name: Lactobacillus ferment

lead: Lactobacillus ferment is made by fermenting with Lactobacillus bacteria and appears in K-beauty and probiotic skincare creams. People use it for barrier support and to calm sensitive or reddened skin so it looks less reactive.

Postbiotic ingredients are proposed to influence the skin microbiome and barrier signalling, though mechanisms for this specific ferment were not shown. The closest human study found was a scalp-microbiome study of a combined Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in daily creams, serums and toners aimed at sensitive or reactive skin, often alongside other barrier and soothing ingredients. Results are typically judged over a few weeks.
No specific harms were documented in the sources reviewed. Postbiotics are not a separate regulatory category and are assessed under existing frameworks case by case.

angle.text: Lactobacillus ferment is a probiotic-derived ingredient in K-beauty creams, used to support the barrier and calm sensitive or reddened skin. Skin looks less reactive as the barrier steadies, though skin-specific human evidence is limited.

lead: Lactobacillus ferment (also listed as Lactobacillus ferment lysate or ferment filtrate) is a cosmetic ingredient made by culturing Lactobacillus bacteria and using the resulting inactivated preparation. It appears in K-beauty and 'probiotic skincare' serums, creams and scalp products, where brands position it for barrier support, soothing and a calmer, more even-looking complexion.[1][2][3]

The idea is that a ferment supplies bacterial fragments and metabolites that support the skin's microbiome and comfort without applying live bacteria; the ISAPP definition describes a postbiotic as a preparation of inanimate microorganisms or their components that confers a health benefit, and Wikipedia describes the research area as emerging and needing confirmation in well-designed human studies.[4] People use these products to reduce visible redness and irritation, which supports an even skin tone and a healthier-looking surface.

Published work specific to Lactobacillus ferment on facial skin is limited. The literature includes a scalp-microbiome study of a combined Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment, a rat study of a Lactobacillus-fermented food supplement, a cosmetic preservation study, and cosmetic patents naming the ingredient in tone-evening and anti-ageing combinations.[5][6][7][2][3]
infobox: Preparation of inactivated microorganisms or components (ISAPP)[4]

paras: Lactobacillus ferment lysate is listed in creams and serums aimed at irritated or barrier-impaired skin. A DailyMed-listed antimicrobial skin cream containing it with edelweiss, calendula and evening primrose extracts lists indications such as relieving redness and burning from impaired barrier function and soothing dry, cracked skin [1].

Patent filings from 2010 describe a method of reducing the appearance of uneven skin tone by applying a composition combining Lactobacillus ferment extract with sunflower seed, kakadu plum and Ferula foetida extracts.[2] A 2011 filing describes skin compositions combining palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, methylsilanol mannuronate and Lactobacillus ferment.[3] Patents describe claims made by applicants, not trial results.

A ferment is produced by growing bacteria in a nutrient medium and then inactivating the culture; lysates additionally break the cells open. Wikipedia's postbiotic page frames inactivated cells and their components as postbiotics, notes that being non-viable avoids infection risks associated with live microbes, and says safety should be assessed case by case, including endotoxin levels and processing residuals.[4]

Fermentation has also been applied to other cosmetic raw materials: a 2026 study fermented jojoba seed cake with Lactobacillus plantarum, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Streptococcus thermophilus to liberate amino acids, peptides and proteins for skin and scalp-care ingredients, examined in 3D tissue models in vitro.[8]

A 2023 study examined a postbiotic Saccharomyces and Lactobacillus ferment complex (SLFC), a Himalaya-derived preparation, on the scalp bacterial and fungal microbiome of Chinese women with sensitive scalp syndrome, in healthy women aged 30 to 45 classified by questionnaire into healthy and sensitive scalp groups, using 16S rRNA and ITS1 sequencing to compare microbial communities and assessing microbiome changes and relief of symptoms [7]. It involved a two-organism ferment, so effects cannot be assigned to Lactobacillus alone.

A registered trial compared a postbiotic gel with placebo for gingival inflammation in people with Down syndrome [9]. No controlled human trial of Lactobacillus ferment for facial wrinkles, tone or acne has been published.

A 2006 rat study of a Lactobacillus ferment of wheat, barley and kefir grains as a food supplement reported smaller body-weight gain on a high-fat diet,[5] and lower perirenal and epididymal fat weights than the high-fat control; this concerns oral nutrition, not skin.

A 2018 study of 13 antimicrobial substances in an oil-in-water cosmetic emulsion examined preservative efficacy using ISO 11930 challenge tests. Most natural-origin substances met the primary criterion, but Lactobacillus ferment did not meet criterion A in the challenge tests with Candida albicans and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so it did not perform as a standalone preservative in that setting.[6]
The reviewed sources report no specific adverse effects for topical Lactobacillus ferment. The DailyMed label lists generic precautions such as keeping out of reach of children [1].
